chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from more than one (narrator), from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm who said:

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to Ismail ibn Muhammad, having mentioned to him that his son had given charity on his behalf: 'He is (still) a man.' He (the Imam) said: 'So command him to give charity, even if it be with a piece of bread.'

Then he (the narrator) said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'A man from the Children of Israel had a son who was beloved to him. Someone came to him in his sleep and said: Your son — on the night he consummates (his marriage) with his wife — will die.'

He said: When that night came and his father had prepared for it, his father feared that prediction. But in the morning, his son was safe. So his father went to him and said: O my dear son! Did you do anything good last night? He said: No, except that a beggar came to the door, and they had stored food for me, so I gave it to the beggar. He (the father) said: By this, God has averted (death) from you.

key_terms.الصدقة: Sadaqa — voluntary charity; here used as a means of averting calamity
key_terms.الكسرة من الخبز: A piece of bread — indicating that even the smallest act of charity carries immense spiritual power
key_terms.بنو إسرائيل: Children of Israel — used as a parabolic frame; Shia hadith literature often employs stories from earlier prophetic traditions to illustrate universal moral truths
key_terms.دفع البلاء: Repelling of affliction — the hadith's core theological point: sadaqa can avert divine decrees of harm

ai.seo_question: Does charity avert death and calamity in Islamic teaching?
ai.summary: This hadith teaches that even a small act of charity — as little as a piece of bread — can avert divinely decreed calamities. Imam al-Ridha (AS) encourages Ismail ibn Muhammad's son to give sadaqa personally, even minimally, to gain its spiritual benefit. He then cites a narrative from Imam al-Baqir (AS) about a man from Bani Isra'il whose son was foretold to die on his wedding night, but was saved by spontaneously giving his own food to a beggar at the door. This illustrates the Shia belief that sadaqa is among the most powerful means of repelling calamity (bala'), a doctrine central to Shia devotional practice.
